account: The Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS) describes ReefScan as a modular suite of automated marine monitoring systems. It integrates machine learning, imaging sensors and robotics and “uses machine learning for real-time object identification and classification, freeing human effort from routine tasks”. AIMS describes ReefCloud as a platform on which users upload survey images, apply automated benthic analysis and generate consistent outputs. AIMS says that ReefCloud “reduces manual processing time” and lets teams focus on interpretation and management actions. On the ReefCloud.ai site, the makers claim that AI image processing gives results “that would take weeks in hours, with up to 90% accuracy”. AIMS lists a 2022 Asia-Pacific Spatial Excellence Award and a Fast Company honorable mention in the AI and Data category. It lists in-kind support from Accenture and the Allen Coral Atlas. AIMS staff wrote in March 2025 that ReefCloud had a network of over 2,000 practitioners in over 90 countries. In August 2025, authors at a Western Australian government fisheries agency and two universities reported that they had built their own image-analysis models. They wrote that externally hosted platforms such as ReefCloud raise questions of data confidentiality for fisheries agencies. An independent team at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology reported in January 2026 that ReefCloud's model annotations agreed poorly with a researcher's. The team used only the human annotations. A preprint whose authors include AIMS staff, posted on 20 August 2026, reports that ReefScan made island-scale reef assessments possible around Erub, Ugar and Mer, and that Traditional Owners chose it as their preferred method. The authors also report that ReefScan underestimated total hard coral cover against diver photo-transects. No cited study links AI detection of crown-of-thorns starfish to a Reef Authority control action. AIMS's crown-of-thorns pages describe research on detection by environmental DNA and on control by chemical cues. Those pages do not describe any use of AI.

ai_role.statement: In Hong Kong, an independent team had ReefCloud's model annotate 20 of 50 points on each photoquadrat while a researcher annotated the other 30. The team found low consistency between the two and used only the human points. In the Torres Strait, a team that included AIMS staff analyzed images from ReefScan, drop cameras and diver photo-transects with machine-learning models. All the methods used the same kind of analysis, so that comparison concerns the collection platform and does not isolate what the AI contributed.

Connecting Indigenous Marine Stewardship with Emerging Technologies to Monitor Coral Reefs. Authorea preprint, doi:10.22541/authorea.15007672/v1, 20 August 2026. The authors include AIMS staff and describe a monitoring program that Meriam peoples co-developed with AIMS, so the preprint is the makers' account. evidence.citation: Gainsford A, Vercelloni J, Cure K, Kennedy E, Jonker MJ, Stephen B, Carlisle M, Gutchen K, Evans-Illidge E (2026). The authors include AIMS staff and describe a monitoring program that Meriam peoples co-developed with AIMS, so the preprint is the makers' account. It reports a statistical comparison of ReefScan with diver and drop-camera surveys around Erub, Ugar and Mer islands, and that the Meriam Traditional Owners chose ReefScan.

data.limitations: The product description does not report a measured management action, restored coral area, or avoided ecological damage. ReefScan and ReefCloud are related but distinct products, and the latter’s “weeks in hours” claim cannot be assigned to ReefScan without validation. Awards and tool availability do not establish ecological benefit. Other retained sources, complete methods, and supplementary material were not rechecked in this pass.

fields.account: The Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS) describes ReefScan as a modular suite of automated marine monitoring systems. It integrates machine learning, imaging sensors and robotics and “uses machine learning for real-time object identification and classification, freeing human effort from routine tasks”. AIMS describes ReefCloud as a platform on which users upload survey images, apply automated benthic analysis and generate consistent outputs. AIMS says that ReefCloud “reduces manual processing time” and lets teams focus on interpretation and management actions. On the ReefCloud.ai site, the makers claim that AI image processing gives results “that would take weeks in hours, with up to 90% accuracy”. AIMS lists a 2022 Asia-Pacific Spatial Excellence Award and a Fast Company honorable mention in the AI and Data category. It lists in-kind support from Accenture and the Allen Coral Atlas. AIMS staff wrote in March 2025 that ReefCloud had a network of over 2,000 practitioners in over 90 countries. In August 2025, authors at a Western Australian government fisheries agency and two universities reported that they had built their own image-analysis models. They wrote that externally hosted platforms such as ReefCloud raise questions of data confidentiality for fisheries agencies. An independent team at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology reported in January 2026 that ReefCloud's model annotations agreed poorly with a researcher's. The team used only the human annotations. A preprint whose authors include AIMS staff, posted on 20 August 2026, reports that ReefScan made island-scale reef assessments possible around Erub, Ugar and Mer, and that Traditional Owners chose it as their preferred method. The authors also report that ReefScan underestimated total hard coral cover against diver photo-transects. No cited study links AI detection of crown-of-thorns starfish to a Reef Authority control action. AIMS's crown-of-thorns pages describe research on detection by environmental DNA and on control by chemical cues. Those pages do not describe any use of AI.
fields.summary: Authors including AIMS staff report that ReefScan surveys made island-scale reef assessments possible; an independent team found that ReefCloud's model annotations agreed poorly with a researcher's.

purpose: Automate classification of reef imagery so that monitoring programs report faster and at larger scale. The claimed benefit is the intended one.

ratings.reason: A preprint whose authors include AIMS staff reports that ReefScan let the Meriam monitoring program assess reefs at island scale, which in-water methods alone could not do.
